Multi-tenant SaaS on Amazon EKS — a walkthrough with receipts

How one 24-line YAML file becomes an isolated, tiered, cost-attributed customer — and how each promise was verified.

sriram-um/saas-on-eks

Built by working through the AWS SaaS on Amazon EKS workshop and then probing the result. Every screenshot below is from that run: the terminal sessions, the Argo CD trees, the live apps and the cost dashboard. The workshop's own instruction pages are deliberately not reproduced here.

  1. Two customers, one codebase
  2. One cluster to manage, one to run
  3. Teaching Kubernetes to speak AWS

  8. What this is, and what it isn't

The problem

Two customers, one codebase

Every company that sells software to more than one customer eventually hits the same wall. Customer A and Customer B want the same product. Neither wants their data anywhere near the other's. One of them pays ten times more and expects that to mean something. And at the end of the month, somebody in finance asks which customer is actually profitable.

You can solve this by running a separate copy of everything per customer. It works, it isolates beautifully, and it bankrupts you — a hundred customers means a hundred databases, a hundred clusters, a hundred things to patch. Or you can run one shared copy and separate tenants in application code, which is cheap and fast until the day a WHERE tenant_id = ? gets forgotten and you are writing a breach disclosure.

This project is the middle path, made concrete. It is a working multi-tenant platform on Amazon EKS where the same container image serves every customer, but the boundaries between them are enforced by infrastructure — the Kubernetes scheduler, the network layer, and IAM — rather than by developer discipline. Cheap customers share. Expensive customers get their own. And which one a customer is comes down to a single word in a single file.

Why it matters

Application-level tenant separation fails silently: the bug is a missing filter, and everything looks fine until it isn't. Infrastructure-level separation fails loudly — the request times out, the API call returns AccessDenied. The whole point of what follows is turning a class of quiet catastrophic bug into a noisy obvious one.

Here is the product. It is a number-guessing game, chosen because it is boring enough to not distract from the architecture, but it does touch everything a real SaaS app touches: a database for players and scores, object storage for avatars, and a generative-AI call for hints.

Now the same application, for a different customer, on a different URL:

Same image. Same code. The tenant name in the header, the BASIC badge, the upgrade prompt, the leaderboard contents and — as we will see — which AI model answers, which database rows are reachable and which node the pod is even allowed to run on, are all derived from tenant context. Nothing is forked per customer.

The shape

One cluster to manage, one to run

Before the walkthrough, the map. Two EKS clusters, each with one job.

The split matters more than it looks. The control plane cluster holds Argo CD and never runs customer code. The data plane cluster runs customer code and holds no deployment machinery. A tenant that somehow escaped its namespace would find itself on a cluster with no credentials for, and no route to, the system that provisions tenants.

Both clusters run EKS Auto Mode, so nodes are Karpenter-managed and the general-purpose and system nodepools come built in:

The interesting part is what is installed on them. kro, ACK and Argo CD are not Helm charts here — they are EKS capabilities, AWS-managed and version-pinned:

Why it matters

This is a small detail with a large consequence for a platform team. The three components the entire platform depends on are somebody else's upgrade problem. You get a version string and a support contract instead of three more repos to babysit.

And the whole system, viewed from one terminal — three repositories, two cluster contexts, two Argo CD applications, six blueprints:

Those two Argo CD applications are the only deployment path that exists. One delivers the platform's blueprints; the other delivers customers.

Expanding the platform application shows its entire job: keep six ResourceGraphDefinition objects in sync with git. These six definitions are what the rest of this page is about — they encode what the word "tenant" means at this company.

Act 1

Teaching Kubernetes to speak AWS

Start from the ordinary. Here is the app deployed the way anyone would deploy it — a namespace, a deployment, a service, an ingress — running against mock data, with no AWS services behind it:

The app needs a DynamoDB table, an S3 bucket, an IAM role and permission to call Bedrock. The conventional answer is Terraform or CloudFormation: a separate tool, a separate state file, a separate pipeline, and a gap between "the infrastructure exists" and "Kubernetes knows about it" that someone has to bridge by copying ARNs around.

AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) closes that gap by making AWS services into Kubernetes resources. Not references to them — the actual API, as CRDs:

Why it matters

tables.dynamodb.services.k8s.aws is a DynamoDB table you create with kubectl apply. That means one tool, one reconciliation loop, and one place to look. It also means AWS resources inherit Kubernetes semantics — owner references, finalizers, and deletion that actually cascades.

Because they are real Kubernetes objects they have real conditions, so you can block until the cloud has caught up. ACK.ResourceSynced is the load-bearing idea in this whole section:

kubectl wait --for=condition=ACK.ResourceSynced \
  tables.dynamodb.services.k8s.aws/gaming-app-table \
  -n gaming --timeout=120s

The last piece is credentials, and it is the part most teams get wrong. No access keys are created here. Instead an EKS Pod Identity association ties the pod's service account to the IAM role, and the pod receives short-lived credentials it never has to store:

We now have the app talking to real AWS services with no static secrets. But look at what that cost: roughly a dozen separate apply and wait commands, in a specific order, with ARNs and names threaded between them by shell variables. Doing that once is a tutorial. Doing it per customer, correctly, forever, is a liability.

Act 2

One object, thirteen resources

kro — the Kube Resource Orchestrator — solves the ordering-and-threading problem. You describe a graph of resources once, declare which fields flow from one into another, and kro derives the dependency order and gives you a brand-new custom resource type that stands for the whole graph.

The blueprint is a ResourceGraphDefinition. Applying one defines a new kind; creating an instance of that kind materialises everything:

Read the ORDER field in that output. It is the topological sort kro worked out on its own:

[kroConfig appnamespace service ingress s3Bucket database configmap
 s3Policy dynamodbPolicy iamRole serviceaccount
 podIdentityAssociation deployment]
Why it matters

Nobody wrote that order down. kro inferred it from the data dependencies — the IAM role must exist before the Pod Identity association can reference it, the bucket must exist before a policy can name its ARN. Encoding dependencies as data rather than as script line-order is what makes this safe to run a thousand times.

One object produced a namespace, deployment, service, ALB ingress, two service accounts, two configmaps, an S3 bucket, a DynamoDB table, an IAM role, two IAM policies and a Pod Identity association. Verifying from inside the running pod, the resource names were wired in for us:

And because kro owns the graph, teardown is symmetric. One delete, and the AWS resources go too — while the platform blueprints stay put:

This is the hinge of the whole project. We have gone from "a dozen careful commands" to "one object". A one-object abstraction is something you can safely hand to an onboarding pipeline.

Act 3

Onboarding is a pull request

Here is the entire contract for a paying customer. Twenty-four lines:

apiVersion: kro.run/v1alpha1
kind: Tenant
metadata:
  name: tenant-004
  labels:
    tenant-id: tenant-004
    tenant-tier: pro
spec:
  tenantId: tenant-004
  tenantName: "Tenant Pro 004"
  tier: pro                          # <-- the entire tiering decision
  version: "latest"
  bucketName: tenant-004-assets
  tableName: gaming-app-tenant-004

The tenant-main blueprint reads spec.tier and routes to one of two packages. TenantBasicPackage puts the customer onto shared infrastructure. TenantProPackage gives them their own. Same input kind, two very different outputs.

Why it matters

This is the commercial model expressed as code. Sales sells a tier; the tier is a string in a YAML file; the string selects a blueprint; the blueprint decides whether the customer shares a node and a database or gets dedicated ones. Nobody translates a contract into infrastructure by hand, which is exactly where that translation usually goes wrong.

The pooled path

Basic tenants share. First the shared pool is created, then three tenants are onboarded — by committing three files:

Argo CD notices the commit and reconciles. Each Tenant expands into a namespace, a workload, an ingress, an IAM role and three scoped policies, and then serves traffic:

The dedicated path

Change one word and commit again. tier: pro selects TenantProPackage, which brings resources the Basic package never creates — an autoscaler, a dedicated bucket, a dedicated table:

Every tier promise, verified:

  • Dedicated nodepool pro-tenant-004, capped at 20 CPU and 40Gi — a hard ceiling on blast radius as much as on spend
  • 3 replicas instead of 1, so a single node failure is not an outage
  • HPA scaling 3 → 10 on 70% CPU / 80% memory targets
  • Dedicated S3 bucket and DynamoDB table rather than a shared table with tenant-prefixed keys
  • A better AI model — nova-lite for Pro against nova-micro for Basic

That last one is the most interesting, because it is the tier difference that maps most directly to a per-request cost. And as the next section shows, it is enforced in IAM — a Basic tenant cannot invoke the Pro model even if the application code asked it to.

Zoomed out, the customer list is now a git history:

Why it matters

Onboarding is a commit, so it inherits everything git already gives you: review before a customer is created, attribution for who created them, and rollback by revert. Offboarding is deleting a file. There is no separate provisioning system to keep honest, because git is the provisioning system.

Act 4

Isolation, and how to prove it

Everything up to here was construction. This section is the part that matters, because an isolation claim you have not tried to break is not a claim, it is a hope.

So each of the four boundaries below is demonstrated by a command that is supposed to fail. The failures are the evidence.

1. Compute — who shares a machine

Basic tenants are packed onto shared nodes; the Pro tenant gets its own. Karpenter nodepool taints make that structural rather than best-effort:

tenant-001 and tenant-002 sit on one node. tenant-004's three pods sit together on a different node, reachable only by workloads that tolerate tenant-pool=pro-tenant-004:NoSchedule. A Basic tenant's pod cannot land on the Pro tenant's hardware because the scheduler will not place it there.

2. Network — who can reach whom

The real test. From inside a pod in tenant-001, reach for tenant-002's service on its ClusterIP. Both namespaces are on the same cluster, the address resolves, the service is listening:

DENIEDtenant-001 → tenant-002 ClusterIP:8080 — Connection timed out, then ECONNRESET

Note the failure mode: a timeout, not a refusal. The packets are dropped rather than rejected, so a hostile tenant cannot even use connection behaviour to map its neighbours.

Egress is an allowlist too. S3 answers; the open internet does not:

ALLOWEDhttps://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com — Status: 307
DENIEDhttps://example.com — ETIMEDOUT

Both results come from one policy, generated per tenant by kro rather than hand-maintained — note managed-by: kro and the domain-name allowlist:

Why it matters

Egress filtering is the control that turns a code-execution bug into a contained incident. An attacker who achieves RCE inside a tenant pod finds they cannot reach their own command-and-control server, cannot curl a payload in, and cannot exfiltrate to anywhere but the four AWS endpoints the tenant legitimately needs.

3. Identity and data — whose rows are whose

Network isolation is not enough on its own, because tenants share AWS services that live outside the cluster. Two tenants using the same DynamoDB table need a boundary that the network layer cannot see. That boundary is IAM: each tenant gets its own role, delivered by Pod Identity, with policies scoped to its own data.

ALLOWEDlist avatars/tenant-001/ from the tenant-001 pod — Objects: 0
DENIEDlist avatars/tenant-002/ from the same pod — AccessDenied

Same bucket, same code, same SDK call — one prefix works and the neighbour's does not. Then the same test against the shared DynamoDB table, plus the tier boundary:

DENIEDGetItem on TENANT#tenant-002#game-001 from tenant-001 — AccessDeniedException
DENIEDBasic tenant invoking the Pro model us.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 — AccessDeniedException
Why it matters

That second denial is the one to dwell on. The tier isn't enforced by a feature flag the application checks — it is enforced by the credentials the pod holds. A bug in the tier middleware, or an attacker who fully controls the Basic tenant's process, still cannot invoke the expensive model. The billing boundary and the security boundary are the same boundary.

4. Runtime — how much damage one tenant can do

The last boundary is the noisy-neighbour problem, which is what makes pooled tenancy frightening. Pod Security Standards are enforced at the namespace level, and quotas cap what a tenant can consume:

DENIEDprivileged pod in tenant-001 — Forbidden: violates PodSecurity "baseline:latest"
DENIEDoversized deployment — admitted, but every pod blocked: maximum cpu usage per Container is 500m

The oversized-deployment case is a nice illustration of layered defence. The Deployment object is accepted — it is just a spec — but the LimitRange stops every pod the ReplicaSet tries to create, and the failure surfaces as events rather than as a node quietly filling up.

Why it matters

Four independent layers, and no single one of them is load-bearing on its own. Break the network policy and IAM still refuses. Break IAM and the network still drops the packets. Compromise the container and Pod Security blocks the escape. That redundancy is the difference between a demo and something you would put a real customer on.

Act 5

Which customer is actually profitable

One question is left, and it is the one that decides whether the pooled model was a good idea: what does each customer cost to serve?

This is genuinely hard in shared infrastructure. A node runs pods from three tenants plus system daemons; the EC2 bill is one line item. Split cost allocation solves it by apportioning each node's cost across the pods that ran on it, weighted by what they actually requested and used. Because every tenant here already has its own namespace and consistent tenant-id labels, that data has somewhere to land:

tenant-004 — the Pro tenant, with its dedicated nodepool and three replicas — costs visibly more than the pooled Basic tenants below it. Which is the correct and expected answer, and that is precisely the point: the architecture and the invoice tell the same story.

Why it matters

Per-tenant cost turns architecture decisions into business decisions. You can price a tier from measurement rather than guesswork, find the customer on a cheap plan who is quietly consuming a fortune, and answer "should this customer be pooled or dedicated?" with a number. Without it, multi-tenancy is a bet you never get to settle.

Closing

What this is, and what it isn't

The platform above genuinely works, and the failures are genuinely enforced. But it was built by following a workshop, and it would be dishonest to present it as production-ready. The gaps worth naming:

  • Single region. No multi-region failover, no cross-region replication for the tenant data stores.
  • Workshop-scale quotas. A 5-pod, 1-CPU namespace ceiling is a teaching number, not a capacity plan.
  • No tenant-facing control plane. Onboarding is a human writing YAML and pushing it. A real product needs an API and a signup flow in front of that, which is a meaningful amount of work.
  • Pooled data isolation depends on correct policy generation. IAM refuses cross-tenant access because the blueprint scoped the policy correctly. That blueprint is now the highest-value code in the repo and deserves tests that assert denial.
  • Nothing here is load-tested. The HPA is configured; it has never been made to work hard.

What the exercise does establish is the shape of the answer. Tenancy defined once as a blueprint rather than per customer. Tiering as a single field that selects between pooled and dedicated. Isolation enforced at four independent layers, each verified by a command that fails. Onboarding as a commit, offboarding as a deletion. And a cost number per customer at the end of it.

The most transferable idea is the smallest one: make the boundaries fail loudly. A timeout and an AccessDenied are worth more than any amount of documentation asserting that tenants are isolated, because they are the only versions of that claim you can re-run tomorrow.
